newsitem.title: CONGO: Mobutu's health hits Zaire talks, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's health hits Zaire talks, rebels advance.

text.p: Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's poor health delayed talks at sea with his civil war foe Laurent Kabila on Friday with officials saying he was not well enough to climb or be flown on board ship.
"The problem is the steep metal steps," said one South African official on the converted ice-breaker SAS Outeniqua, where Nelson Mandela waited to host the meeting.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but prostate cancer and a whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on power.

As he waited in Congo's port of Pointe Noire to board the Outeniqua, Kabila's rebels flew troops, artillery and other supplies towards the forward base which is a springboard for their march on the capital Kinshasa.

On the humanitarian front, an airlift to repatriate up to 100,000 sick and dying Rwandan Hutu refugees from northeastern Zaire gathered pace as the rebels promised to cooperate with U.N. relief agencies.

"We are dealing with two outstanding leaders who are conscious of the importance of an amicable settlement which will satisfy both of them as well as the people of Zaire," Mandela told reporters on the Russian-built Outeniqua.

"I am confident the two leaders realise the importance of a peaceful settlement," he said, adding: "I know few leaders who have made military gains and nevertheless been committed to peace as Mr Kabila has."
Mandela met Mobutu in Pointe Noire, where the Outeniqua was moored. Mobutu, who has cancer, had been due to board with Mandela but remained on shore.
Kabila was in Angola's capital Luanda holding talks with President Eduardo dos Santos, government sources there said.
He and Mandela's deputy Thabo Mbeki were to take a helicopter to join Mobutu and Mandela on the Outeniqua in international waters off Soyo by the Angolan-Zaire border.
"We are prepared to stay on that ship as long as it takes to reach some conclusions," Mbeki told reporters in Luanda.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis living there, control about three quarters of Zaire.
Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must stand down after three decades in power and has refused to declare a truce for the talks.
Confusion over timing has plagued the runup to the meeting, which diplomats see as a last chance to avert a potentially bloody battle for Zaire's capital of five million people.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.

A commander at rebel headquarters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi said an airlift to the towns of Kikwit and Kananga began on Thursday and rebel forces were about to enter Kenge, the biggest town before Kinshasa.
Hundreds of chanting rebels boarded Boeing 737s, 727s and Fokkers and officers said they were going for the final push.

Mobutu's camp says the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow the veteran strongman to stand down with dignity.
Kabila insists Mobutu must go. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who helped Mandela bring the two sides together, has said there are no conditions for the talks.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in August, has towered over what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries virtually since independence from Belgium in 1960.
Opponents denounce rampant corruption and administrative chaos and accuse Mobutu and his entourage of amassing fortunes while the bulk of the population floundered in poverty.
